question:
Consider the differential equations
(i) $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+2y}{2x-y}$
(ii) $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+2y+1}{2x-y}$.
Determine which equation is homogeneous and justify your answer mathematically.
explanation:
Step 1: Test equation (i)
For $$F(x,y)=\frac{x+2y}{2x-y},$$ divide numerator and denominator by $x$: $$F(x,y)=\frac{1+2\frac{y}{x}}{2-\frac{y}{x}}.$$ Thus, $F(x,y)$ depends only on $\frac{y}{x}$ and is homogeneous of degree zero.
Step 2: Verify by scaling
Also, $$F(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\frac{\lambda x+2\lambda y}{2\lambda x-\lambda y}=F(x,y).$$ Hence, equation (i) is homogeneous.
Step 3: Test equation (ii)
For $$G(x,y)=\frac{x+2y+1}{2x-y},$$ replacing $x,y$ by $\lambda x,\lambda y$ gives $$G(\lambda x,\lambda y)=\frac{\lambda x+2\lambda y+1}{2\lambda x-\lambda y},$$ which is not equal to $G(x,y)$ in general.
Step 4: Conclusion
Therefore, equation (i) is homogeneous, whereas equation (ii) is not homogeneous.

options.B: Only (ii) is homogeneous because of the constant term $1$.
options.D: Only (i) is homogeneous; (ii) is not homogeneous because of the added constant $1$.
